meaning: A class of works teaching magical and mystical formularies, mostly cast as dialogues between Śiva and Durgā; hence the esoteric systems of doctrine and ritual founded upon them.

phonemes.desc: From √tan, “to stretch, extend, weave” — the same root as “tan” and “tend”.
The instrumental suffix: the tantra is the “loom” or “warp” — the extended doctrine.
The word names both the scripture-class and the ritual systems those scriptures teach.

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: tantra — the warp of a loom, the system’s threads

pronunciation.note: The word is a weaving-metaphor: the tantra is the warp into which the practice’s threads are stretched.

domains.title: The Loom of Esoteric Doctrine
domains.subtitle: The Extended System, Scripture and Practice
domains.lead: Tantra is the name of a scripture-class and the ritual systems those scriptures teach: works cast as dialogues between Śiva and the Goddess, embracing mantra, mandala, initiation, and the disciplined transgression of ordinary purity-rules. From the sixth-century Śaiva scriptures to Tibetan Vajrayāna, the tantras are the Indian religions’ most ambitious technology for accelerated transformation.

cards.name: The Scripture-Dialogue
cards.desc: The tantra is cast as Śiva’s answer to the Goddess’s questions — god and power, doctrine and energy, in conversation.

cards.name: The Maṇḍala
cards.desc: The deity’s palace-diagram, constructed from coloured sands or drawn, entered by initiation through the four gates.

cards.name: Mantra and Mudrā
cards.desc: Sound and gesture: the mantra pronounced, the hand-seal struck — the body made instrument of the doctrine.

cards.name: Transgression as Method
cards.desc: The pañcamakāra — the five M’s — consumed in ritual under vow, inverting purity to burn through it.

mythology.lead: Tantra’s mythology is its own theology of secrecy and speed: the god teaching the Goddess, the guru initiating the disciple, and the householder’s body becoming the ritual ground. Its stories are the scriptures’ frames — Śiva on Mount Kailāsa answering Pārvatī’s midnight questions, the siddhas flying on mantra-power, the kings protected by Śaiva rites.

myths.title: The God Teaches the Goddess
myths.text: Nearly every tantra opens on a mountain: Śiva, asked by the Goddess how liberation may be quick for the poor in merit and short in life, answers with the system. The gender of the exchange is the doctrine — the god is knowledge, the Goddess is energy, and the tantra is their union written down for the age of decline.

myths.title: The Clan-Traditions
myths.text: The early Śaiva tantras organised themselves as kulas, clans — initiatory lineages bound to a deity, a mantra, and a guru. The clans’ mythology made heroes of the siddhas, the perfected ones who flew, stayed young, and turned the elements — the tantras’ advertisements and their cautionary tales.

myths.title: The Thunderbolt Vehicle
myths.text: Buddhism absorbed the tantras wholesale: the Vajrayāna made the Buddha speak as Vajradhara, the thunderbolt-holder, and taught that buddhahood could be won in a single lifetime. The Tibetan canons — Kanjur and Tanjur — are the largest single body of tantric scripture preserved anywhere.

myths.title: The State of the Rites
myths.text: Medieval kings ruled by tantra: the Śaiva rites of protection (rakṣā) and the pacificatory rites (śānti) were statecraft. The inscriptions of the Cōḻas and the Pālas record land-grants to tantric monasteries that anchored their realms — the esoteric schools as the polity’s immune system.

lore.syncretism: Tantra swallowed its rivals: Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta, and Buddhist tantras share a grammar of mantra, mandala, and initiation beneath their rival theologies. The Śākta tantras made the Goddess the system’s core; the Tibetan schools fused the whole into Vajrayāna; and modern global ‘tantra’ is a Western distillation of one strand of a much larger river.
lore.culturalLegacy: The maṇḍala entered the world’s art-vocabulary; the mantra and the mudrā passed into global practice. Tantra’s academic rediscovery in the twentieth century rewrote the history of Hinduism and Buddhism — the ‘esoteric’ is now standard curriculum. And the word, in the West, became a byword for sacred sexuality, a reduction the tradition itself would barely recognize.
lore.extendedMeditation: Tantra: the warp stretched on the loom, restored in plain letters that hold nothing back and reveal nothing. The name is the method — the system extended, thread by thread, until the whole fabric shows the pattern. Two syllables, one loom, every thread.
lore.archaeology: Tantra leaves mandalas: the Borobudur’s galleries, the painted maṇḍala-halls of Alchi and Tabo, and the stūpa-temples of the Himalayan lineages. The colossal Hevajra and Cakrasaṃvara images of Khmer art are its royal monuments.
lore.cult: The guru is the cult: initiation (dīkṣā) admits the practitioner to the clan, and the daily sādhana — the deity’s self-generation by mantra and visualization — is the liturgy. The fire-rites (homa) burn the offerings that seal the pacts.
lore.iconography: The deity in union — the yab-yum of Tibet, the Śiva-Śakti of the Hindu tantras — the two-in-one that images the doctrine. The vajra, the bell, the skull-cup, and the curved knife are the instruments; the mandala is the ground.
lore.reception: Religious studies treats tantra as the field’s great twentieth-century discovery — the recovery of the esoteric half of Asian religion. The Western ‘Tantra’ of the counterculture is a case-study in selective reception: one limb of the system, exported as the whole body.
